stem: Which list gives the defining properties of a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal F$ on a set $\Omega$?
correct: $\Omega\in\mathcal F$, $\mathcal F$ is closed under complements, and closed under countable unions.
$\mathcal F$ contains $\Omega$, and $A\in\mathcal F$ implies $A^c\in\mathcal F$, and $A_1,A_2,\dots\in\mathcal F$ implies $\bigcup_n A_n\in\mathcal F$.

distractors.text: $\Omega\in\mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under complements and under finite unions only.
distractors.misconception: describes an algebra of sets; a $\sigma$-algebra needs countable unions

distractors.text: $\Omega\in\mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under complements and under arbitrary unions of its sets.
distractors.misconception: asks for arbitrary unions, which is the property of a topology

distractors.text: $\Omega\in\mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under countable unions and countable intersections only.
distractors.misconception: omits closure under complements, which is essential

distractors.text: $\Omega\in\mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under complements and under countable disjoint unions only.
distractors.misconception: describes a Dynkin system, which is weaker than a $\sigma$-algebra

distractors.text: $\mathcal F$ contains every subset of $\Omega$, so that any set can be assigned a probability.
distractors.misconception: takes the power set to be the only $\sigma$-algebra

explanation: A $\sigma$-algebra contains $\Omega$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (hence countable intersections). Closure under finite unions only gives an algebra, closure under disjoint unions gives a Dynkin system, and the power set is only one example.

stem: Which requirement distinguishes a probability measure $P$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ from a finitely additive set function?
correct: Additivity holds for every countable sequence of pairwise disjoint events, not merely for finite ones.
$P(\bigcup_n A_n)=\sum_n P(A_n)$ for pairwise disjoint events $A_1,A_2,\dots$, together with $P(\Omega)=1$.

distractors.text: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$ holds for every pair of events, whether or not they are disjoint.
distractors.misconception: forgets that additivity needs disjointness (inclusion-exclusion otherwise)

distractors.text: $P(A)>0$ for every non-empty event $A$, so that each possible outcome has positive probability.
distractors.misconception: confuses non-empty with non-null; events can have probability zero

distractors.text: $P$ is defined on every subset of $\Omega$, so that no restriction to a $\sigma$-algebra is needed.
distractors.misconception: ignores that measures are defined only on a $\sigma$-algebra

distractors.text: $P(A)=1-P(A^c)$ for every event $A$, which is the only property needed besides $P(\Omega)=1$.
distractors.misconception: takes a consequence of the axioms for the axiom of additivity

distractors.text: $P$ takes only the values $0$ and $1$ on events that are disjoint, so that overlaps never occur.
distractors.misconception: invents a restriction on values of $P$ for disjoint events

explanation: Countable additivity on disjoint events, with $P(\Omega)=1$ and $P\ge0$, is what makes limits of events behave well. Finite additivity alone does not give continuity of $P$ along monotone sequences of events.

stem: For a collection $\mathcal C$ of subsets of $\Omega$, what is the $\sigma$-algebra $\sigma(\mathcal C)$ generated by $\mathcal C$?
correct: The smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ that contains every one of the sets in $\mathcal C$.
The intersection of all $\sigma$-algebras on $\Omega$ that contain the whole collection $\mathcal C$.

distractors.text: The collection of all countable unions of sets in $\mathcal C$, taken in a single step.
distractors.misconception: forgets complements and repeated operations; this collection need not be closed

distractors.text: The union of all $\sigma$-algebras on $\Omega$ that contain every set in $\mathcal C$.
distractors.misconception: swaps union with intersection; that union is not even a $\sigma$-algebra

distractors.text: The largest $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ whose sets can all be built out of the sets of $\mathcal C$.
distractors.misconception: confuses smallest containing $\mathcal C$ with a largest collection

distractors.text: The collection of all complements and finite unions of sets in $\mathcal C$, which is always enough.
distractors.misconception: stops at the algebra generated by $\mathcal C$, missing countable unions

distractors.text: The collection of sets $A$ whose probability $P(A)$ is determined by the values of $P$ on $\mathcal C$.
distractors.misconception: mixes the generated $\sigma$-algebra with a uniqueness statement about measures

explanation: $\sigma(\mathcal C)$ is the intersection of all $\sigma$-algebras containing $\mathcal C$; it is the smallest one. One round of complements and unions generally does not produce a $\sigma$-algebra.

stem: Let $\mathcal F_1$ and $\mathcal F_2$ be $\sigma$-algebras on the same set $\Omega$. Which statement is correct?
correct: $\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2$ is always a $\sigma$-algebra, but $\mathcal F_1\cup\mathcal F_2$ need not be one.
The intersection of any family of $\sigma$-algebras on $\Omega$ is a $\sigma$-algebra; the union of two of them can fail to be closed under unions.

distractors.text: Both $\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2$ and $\mathcal F_1\cup\mathcal F_2$ are always $\sigma$-algebras on $\Omega$.
distractors.misconception: assumes closure under unions of collections, which fails

distractors.text: $\mathcal F_1\cup\mathcal F_2$ is always a $\sigma$-algebra, but $\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2$ need not be one.
distractors.misconception: reverses which of the two operations preserves the structure

distractors.text: Neither $\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2$ nor $\mathcal F_1\cup\mathcal F_2$ is a $\sigma$-algebra unless $\mathcal F_1=\mathcal F_2$.
distractors.misconception: thinks identical collections are needed for any combination to work

distractors.text: $\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2$ is a $\sigma$-algebra only when $\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2$ or $\mathcal F_2\subseteq\mathcal F_1$.
distractors.misconception: adds a nesting condition that intersections do not need

distractors.text: $\mathcal F_1\cup\mathcal F_2$ is a $\sigma$-algebra whenever both are finite collections of subsets of $\Omega$.
distractors.misconception: believes finiteness repairs closure under unions

explanation: Each axiom is inherited by an intersection. A union can fail: with $\Omega=\{1,2,3\}$, $\{\{1\}\}$ and $\{\{2\}\}$ generate $\sigma$-algebras whose union lacks $\{1,2\}$.

stem: Which statement about the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ is correct?
correct: It is generated by the open sets of $\mathbb R$, and it is strictly smaller than the power set of $\mathbb R$.
It is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing all open intervals, and some subsets of $\mathbb R$ are not Borel.

distractors.text: It consists of all subsets of $\mathbb R$, because every set can be approximated by open sets.
distractors.misconception: assumes every subset of the line is Borel

distractors.text: It is exactly the collection of countable unions of open intervals, which are the open sets.
distractors.misconception: identifies the Borel sets with the open sets

distractors.text: It is exactly the collection of open sets together with the closed sets of $\mathbb R$.
distractors.misconception: forgets closure under countable operations; $G_\delta$ sets are Borel but neither open nor closed

distractors.text: It is the collection of all Lebesgue measurable subsets of $\mathbb R$, so the two coincide.
distractors.misconception: identifies Borel with Lebesgue measurable; the latter is strictly larger

distractors.text: It is generated by the single points $\{x\}$, since every Borel set is a countable union of points.
distractors.misconception: the $\sigma$-algebra of countable and co-countable sets is generated by points, not the Borel one

explanation: $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ is generated by open sets (equivalently by intervals $(-\infty,a]$). Not every subset is Borel, and the Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebra is strictly larger than the Borel one.

stem: What does it mean for $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ to be a random variable on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$?
correct: For every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, the preimage $\{X\in B\}$ is an event belonging to $\mathcal F$.
The sets $\{X\le a\}$ are events of $\mathcal F$ for every real number $a$, which gives all Borel preimages.

distractors.text: For every set $A\in\mathcal F$, the image $X(A)$ is a Borel subset of $\mathbb R$.
distractors.misconception: swaps preimages with images

distractors.text: $X$ is a continuous function on $\Omega$, so that small changes of $\omega$ change $X$ only slightly.
distractors.misconception: confuses measurability with continuity; $\Omega$ need not carry a topology

distractors.text: $X$ takes only finitely many values, so that each value $\{X=x\}$ is an event of $\mathcal F$.
distractors.misconception: restricts to simple functions

distractors.text: For every subset $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, the preimage $\{X\in B\}$ belongs to $\mathcal F$.
distractors.misconception: asks for all subsets rather than all Borel sets

distractors.text: The expectation $E[X]$ exists and is finite, so that $X$ can be integrated against $P$.
distractors.misconception: confuses being a random variable with integrability

explanation: Measurability is about preimages of Borel sets (it is enough to check the sets $(-\infty,a]$). Continuity, finiteness of values and integrability are separate properties.

stem: What is the distribution (law) $\mu_X$ of a random variable $X$?
correct: The probability measure on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ given by $\mu_X(B)=P(X\in B)$, the pushforward of $P$.
The measure on the Borel sets of the line that records how much probability $X$ puts on each Borel set.

distractors.text: The probability measure $P$ on $\Omega$ itself, which $X$ merely relabels with real numbers.
distractors.misconception: confuses the law on $\mathbb R$ with the original measure on $\Omega$

distractors.text: The function $x\mapsto P(X=x)$, which exists and determines the law for every random variable.
distractors.misconception: assumes a probability mass function always exists

distractors.text: The function $\omega\mapsto X(\omega)$ itself, since the law and the random variable carry the same information.
distractors.misconception: identifies the law with the random variable

distractors.text: The collection $\{X^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$ of events, without any measure attached.
distractors.misconception: confuses the law with the generated $\sigma$-algebra $\sigma(X)$

distractors.text: The measure on $\Omega$ defined by $A\mapsto E[X\,1_A]$, which weights events by the values of $X$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the law with a measure with density $X$ with respect to $P$

explanation: $\mu_X=P\circ X^{-1}$ lives on $\mathbb R$. It always exists, even when there is no density or mass function, and it forgets which $\omega$ produced which value.

stem: Random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution. Which conclusion is justified?
correct: $E[g(X)]=E[g(Y)]$ for every Borel $g$ with finite expectations, but $X$ and $Y$ need not be equal.
They give the same expectations of functions, yet $X=Y$ can fail with positive probability.

distractors.text: $X=Y$ almost surely, because equal laws force equal values at almost every $\omega$.
distractors.misconception: confuses equality in law with almost sure equality

distractors.text: $X$ and $Y$ are independent, because identical laws leave no information to share between them.
distractors.misconception: confuses identical distribution with independence

distractors.text: $\sigma(X)=\sigma(Y)$, so both generate the same collection of events on $\Omega$.
distractors.misconception: thinks equal laws give equal generated $\sigma$-algebras

distractors.text: $X$ and $Y$ must be defined on the same probability space, since their laws are compared there.
distractors.misconception: believes the comparison of laws needs a common sample space

distractors.text: $E[g(X)]=E[g(Y)]$ only for bounded $g$, because unbounded $g$ would need the original variables.
distractors.misconception: thinks equal laws give equal expectations only for bounded functions

explanation: Expectations of $g(X)$ depend only on the law of $X$. But $X\sim N(0,1)$ and $-X$ have the same law and differ almost surely; and laws can be compared across different spaces.

stem: When is a random variable $Y$ measurable with respect to $\sigma(X)$, the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $X$?
correct: Exactly when $Y=g(X)$ for some Borel function $g$ (the Doob-Dynkin lemma).
When $Y$ is a function of $X$ alone: $Y(\omega)=g(X(\omega))$ with $g$ Borel measurable.

distractors.text: Exactly when $Y$ is independent of $X$, since $\sigma(X)$ then carries no information about $Y$.
distractors.misconception: confuses measurability (full information) with independence (none)

distractors.text: Exactly when $Y=X$ almost surely, because only $X$ itself is measurable with respect to $\sigma(X)$.
distractors.misconception: thinks only $X$ is measurable with respect to its own $\sigma$-algebra

distractors.text: Exactly when $Y=g(X)$ for a continuous function $g$, because Borel functions are too general.
distractors.misconception: restricts $g$ to continuous functions unnecessarily

distractors.text: Exactly when $Y$ and $X$ have the same law, so that they generate the same distribution.
distractors.misconception: confuses measurability with equality in law

distractors.text: Exactly when $Y$ is bounded and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\ne0$, so that $X$ explains $Y$.
distractors.misconception: replaces measurability with a correlation condition

explanation: Doob-Dynkin: $Y$ is $\sigma(X)$-measurable iff $Y=g(X)$ for Borel $g$. Such a $Y$ is completely determined by $X$, the opposite of independence.

stem: $X$ is a random variable and $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a function. When is $g(X)$ guaranteed to be a random variable?
correct: When $g$ is Borel measurable, which includes every continuous function and every monotone function.
Whenever $g^{-1}(B)$ is a Borel set for every Borel set $B$, since then $\{g(X)\in B\}=\{X\in g^{-1}(B)\}\in\mathcal F$.

distractors.text: For every function $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, because $X$ is already measurable and $g$ only relabels values.
distractors.misconception: ignores that $g$ itself must be measurable

distractors.text: Only when $g$ is continuous, because measurable functions that are not continuous would not preserve events.
distractors.misconception: restricts to continuous functions; Borel functions suffice

distractors.text: Only when $g$ is injective, so that distinct values of $X$ remain distinct after applying $g$.
distractors.misconception: thinks injectivity is needed

distractors.text: Only when $g$ is differentiable, since a derivative is needed to transport the law of $X$.
distractors.misconception: asks for differentiability, which only matters for density formulas

distractors.text: Only when $E[g(X)]$ is finite, because a random variable must have a finite mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses being a random variable with integrability

explanation: $\{g(X)\in B\}=\{X\in g^{-1}(B)\}$ is an event when $g^{-1}(B)$ is Borel. A non-Borel $g$ can break this, and injectivity, differentiability or integrability are irrelevant.

stem: How is the expectation $E[X]=\int X\,dP$ of a random variable defined in the Lebesgue approach?
correct: By simple functions: a supremum for $X\ge0$, then $E[X]=E[X^+]-E[X^-]$ when this is defined.
Take the supremum of $\sum a_iP(A_i)$ over simple functions below $X\ge0$, then split $X=X^+-X^-$.

distractors.text: As the sum $\sum_x xP(X=x)$ over the values of $X$, which is valid for every random variable.
distractors.misconception: applies the discrete formula to all random variables, including continuous ones

distractors.text: As the Riemann integral of $X$ over $\Omega$, which exists for every measurable function $X$.
distractors.misconception: confuses Lebesgue with Riemann integration; $\Omega$ need not even be an interval

distractors.text: As $\int x f(x)\,dx$, which requires that $X$ has a density and cannot be defined otherwise.
distractors.misconception: thinks the expectation needs a density

distractors.text: As the infimum over simple functions lying above $X$, defined for every random variable.
distractors.misconception: uses upper approximation and ignores the sign decomposition

distractors.text: As $E[X]=E[X^+]-E[X^-]$ for every $X$, including when both parts are infinite, with value $0$.
distractors.misconception: treats $\infty-\infty$ as defined

explanation: The integral is built in stages: simple functions, non-negative functions via a supremum, then general $X=X^+-X^-$. If both $E[X^+]$ and $E[X^-]$ are infinite, $E[X]$ is undefined.

stem: Which statement is the monotone convergence theorem for expectations?
correct: If $0\le X_n\uparrow X$ almost surely, then $E[X_n]\uparrow E[X]$, with no integrability condition.
Non-negative variables increasing to $X$ have expectations increasing to $E[X]$, even if infinite.

distractors.text: If $X_n\to X$ almost surely, then $E[X_n]\to E[X]$, with no further condition on the sequence.
distractors.misconception: drops monotonicity, which is the whole point of the theorem

distractors.text: If $0\le X_n\downarrow X$ almost surely, then $E[X_n]\downarrow E[X]$, without any integrability condition.
distractors.misconception: applies the theorem to decreasing sequences, where $E[X_1]$ may be infinite

distractors.text: If $0\le X_n\uparrow X$ and the $X_n$ are uniformly bounded, then $E[X_n]\to E[X]$ only then.
distractors.misconception: adds boundedness as a requirement

distractors.text: If $X_n\uparrow X$ uniformly on $\Omega$, then $E[X_n]\to E[X]$, which is why monotonicity is needed.
distractors.misconception: replaces almost sure convergence by uniform convergence

distractors.text: If $0\le X_n\uparrow X$, then $E[X_n]\uparrow E[X]$ provided that $E[X]<\infty$ is known beforehand.
distractors.misconception: adds finiteness of the limit; the theorem allows $E[X]=\infty$

explanation: MCT needs only $0\le X_n\uparrow X$ a.s.; the limit may have infinite expectation. For decreasing sequences or non-monotone ones the conclusion can fail.

stem: What does Fatou's lemma say about non-negative random variables $X_n$?
correct: $E[\liminf_n X_n]\le\liminf_n E[X_n]$, and the inequality can be strict.
The expectation of the lower limit is at most the lower limit of the expectations.

distractors.text: $E[\liminf_n X_n]\ge\liminf_n E[X_n]$, so the expectation of a limit is always the larger.
distractors.misconception: reverses the inequality

distractors.text: $E[\liminf_n X_n]=\liminf_n E[X_n]$ always, so that equality holds for all non-negative sequences.
distractors.misconception: turns the inequality into an equality, which is the content of convergence theorems

distractors.text: $E[\limsup_n X_n]\le\limsup_n E[X_n]$, which holds without any further assumption on the sequence.
distractors.misconception: swaps liminf for limsup; this direction needs domination

distractors.text: $E[\liminf_n X_n]\le\liminf_n E[X_n]$ for all real $X_n$, with no sign condition needed.
distractors.misconception: drops the non-negativity assumption

distractors.text: $\liminf_n E[X_n]\le E[X]$ whenever $X_n\to X$ almost surely, for any sign of $X_n$.
distractors.misconception: mixes up the direction and the sign assumption

explanation: Fatou needs $X_n\ge0$ and gives only an inequality: mass can disappear in the limit, as for $X_n=n1_{(0,1/n)}$ on $[0,1]$, where $E[\liminf X_n]=0<1=\lim E[X_n]$.

stem: How can $E[g(X)]$ be computed, for a Borel function $g$ and a random variable $X$ with law $\mu_X$?
correct: As $\int g\,d\mu_X$, an integral over $\mathbb R$ with respect to the law of $X$, whenever $g(X)$ is integrable.
By the change of variables formula $E[g(X)]=\int_{\mathbb R}g(x)\,\mu_X(dx)$, which needs no density of $X$.

distractors.text: As $g(E[X])$, since taking the expectation commutes with applying any function to $X$.
distractors.misconception: assumes $E[g(X)]=g(E[X])$, which holds only for affine $g$

distractors.text: As $\int g(x)f_X(x)\,dx$, which requires that $X$ has a density $f_X$ with respect to Lebesgue measure.
distractors.misconception: thinks the formula needs a density

distractors.text: As $\int g\,d\mu_X$ only when $g$ is monotone, so that the change of variables is valid.
distractors.misconception: adds a monotonicity condition to the change of variables

distractors.text: As $\int g(X(\omega))\,d\mu_X(\omega)$, integrating over $\Omega$ against the law of $X$.
distractors.misconception: mixes the sample space $\Omega$ with the line $\mathbb R$

distractors.text: As $\sum_x g(x)P(X=x)$, which is valid for every random variable $X$ and every Borel $g$.
distractors.misconception: applies the discrete formula to all random variables

explanation: The pushforward identity $E[g(X)]=\int g\,d\mu_X$ holds for every random variable and Borel $g$. A density is a convenience, not a requirement, and $g(E[X])$ is generally different (Jensen).

stem: A random variable satisfies $X\ge0$ and $E[X]=0$. What follows?
correct: $X=0$ almost surely, although $X(\omega)$ may be positive for some $\omega$ in a set of probability zero.
$P(X>0)=0$, so $X$ vanishes except possibly on a null set.

distractors.text: $X(\omega)=0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$, because a non-negative variable with zero mean has no positive values.
distractors.misconception: confuses almost sure with sure equality

distractors.text: $P(X>0)>0$ is still possible, as long as the positive values of $X$ are small enough on average.
distractors.misconception: misses that $E[X]\ge\epsilon P(X\ge\epsilon)$ forces $P(X\ge\epsilon)=0$

distractors.text: $X$ must take both positive and negative values, so that its mean can vanish.
distractors.misconception: ignores the hypothesis $X\ge0$

distractors.text: $X$ must be bounded, because an unbounded non-negative variable has an infinite mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses unbounded with non-integrable

distractors.text: $X=0$ almost surely only if $X$ also takes finitely many values, such as a simple function.
distractors.misconception: restricts the conclusion to simple functions

explanation: By Markov, $P(X\ge\epsilon)\le E[X]/\epsilon=0$ for every $\epsilon>0$, so $P(X>0)=0$. But $X$ can differ from $0$ on a null set.

stem: Which hypotheses make the dominated convergence theorem valid?
correct: $X_n\to X$ almost surely and $|X_n|\le Y$ for all $n$ with $E[Y]<\infty$; then $E[X_n]\to E[X]$.
A single integrable dominating variable $Y$ above every $|X_n|$, together with almost sure convergence of the $X_n$.

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ almost surely and $\sup_n E|X_n|<\infty$; boundedness in $L^1$ is enough for the conclusion.
distractors.misconception: replaces domination by $L^1$-boundedness, which does not suffice

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ in distribution and $|X_n|\le Y$ with $E[Y]<\infty$, since distributions determine expectations.
distractors.misconception: weakens almost sure convergence to convergence in distribution

distractors.text: $X_n\uparrow X$ is monotone and $|X_n|\le Y$ with $E[Y]=\infty$ allowed, since monotonicity does the work.
distractors.misconception: allows non-integrable dominating variables

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ almost surely and each $X_n$ is integrable; integrability of each term is enough.
distractors.misconception: misses that a uniform integrable bound is needed

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ uniformly and $|X_n|\le Y$ for a variable $Y$ that may depend on $n$.
distractors.misconception: allows the dominating variable to depend on $n$

explanation: DCT needs a.s. convergence and one integrable $Y$ with $|X_n|\le Y$ for all $n$. Boundedness in $L^1$ is weaker and fails for $X_n=n1_{(0,1/n)}$.

stem: What does the example $X_n=n\,1_{(0,1/n)}$ on $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure show?
correct: Almost sure convergence $X_n\to0$ does not imply $E[X_n]\to E[0]$: mass can concentrate on shrinking sets.
The pointwise limit is $0$, yet $E[X_n]$ stays at the value $1$, so some domination or uniform integrability is needed.

distractors.text: Fatou's lemma fails for non-negative sequences, because $E[\liminf X_n]$ exceeds $\liminf E[X_n]$ here.
distractors.misconception: misreads the direction; Fatou holds and the inequality is strict here

distractors.text: The dominated convergence theorem fails, even though the $X_n$ are dominated by an integrable function.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that no integrable dominating function exists for this sequence

distractors.text: Monotone convergence fails, even though $0\le X_n\uparrow X$ almost surely is satisfied by this sequence.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that this sequence is not monotone

distractors.text: Almost sure convergence never gives convergence of expectations, whatever extra hypotheses are available.
distractors.misconception: overgeneralises; domination or uniform integrability repairs it

distractors.text: The sequence $X_n$ does not converge almost surely, since its values grow without bound.
distractors.misconception: thinks unbounded values prevent pointwise convergence; each $\omega$ eventually has $X_n(\omega)=0$

explanation: For each $\omega$, $X_n(\omega)=0$ once $n>1/\omega$, so $X_n\to0$ a.s., but $E[X_n]=1$. No integrable $Y$ dominates all $X_n$, and the family is not uniformly integrable.

stem: Which condition defines uniform integrability of a family $(X_n)$?
correct: $\sup_n E\big[|X_n|\,1_{\{|X_n|>K\}}\big]\to0$ as $K\to\infty$.
The tails of $|X_n|$ contribute uniformly little: $\lim_{K\to\infty}\sup_n E[|X_n|;|X_n|>K]=0$.

distractors.text: $\sup_n E|X_n|<\infty$, so that the sequence is bounded in $L^1$ and nothing else is needed.
distractors.misconception: confuses $L^1$-boundedness with uniform integrability

distractors.text: $|X_n|\le K$ for every $n$ and a single constant $K$, so that the family is uniformly bounded.
distractors.misconception: takes uniform boundedness, which is sufficient but not necessary

distractors.text: Each $X_n$ is integrable, $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, which makes the whole family uniformly integrable.
distractors.misconception: confuses integrability of each term with uniformity over the family

distractors.text: $E|X_n|\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, so that the sequence converges to zero in $L^1$.
distractors.misconception: confuses uniform integrability with $L^1$ convergence

distractors.text: $\sup_n E\big[|X_n|\,1_{\{|X_n|>K\}}\big]<\infty$ for some $K$, which is the same as $L^1$-boundedness.
distractors.misconception: drops the limit $K\to\infty$, which is what makes the condition uniform

explanation: Uniform integrability requires the tail contributions to vanish uniformly in $n$. It implies $L^1$-boundedness but not conversely, and uniform boundedness implies it but is not required.

stem: Which statement links convergence in probability, uniform integrability and $L^1$ convergence?
correct: If $X_n\to X$ in probability and $(X_n)$ is uniformly integrable, then $X_n\to X$ in $L^1$.
Uniform integrability upgrades convergence in probability to $L^1$ convergence (Vitali), so expectations converge.

distractors.text: If $X_n\to X$ in probability and $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$, then $X_n\to X$ in $L^1$.
distractors.misconception: replaces uniform integrability by $L^1$-boundedness

distractors.text: Uniform integrability of $(X_n)$ alone implies $X_n\to X$ almost surely for some random variable $X$.
distractors.misconception: thinks uniform integrability gives any kind of pointwise convergence

distractors.text: If $E[X_n]\to E[X]$ then $(X_n)$ must be uniformly integrable, so the two are equivalent.
distractors.misconception: reverses the implication; expectations can converge without uniform integrability

distractors.text: Uniform integrability is needed only for almost sure convergence, not for convergence in probability.
distractors.misconception: misplaces the role of uniform integrability

distractors.text: If $X_n\to X$ in $L^1$, then $(X_n)$ cannot be uniformly integrable, since the tails vanish.
distractors.misconception: reverses the true fact that $L^1$ convergence implies uniform integrability

explanation: Vitali's theorem: convergence in probability plus uniform integrability is equivalent to convergence in $L^1$. $L^1$ convergence in turn implies uniform integrability.

stem: When can the expectation of an infinite sum be computed termwise, $E\big[\sum_nX_n\big]=\sum_nE[X_n]$?
correct: Always when every $X_n\ge0$ (monotone convergence), and for signed terms when $\sum_nE|X_n|<\infty$.
For non-negative terms with no extra condition; for general terms one needs absolute summability $\sum_nE|X_n|<\infty$.

distractors.text: Always, for terms of any sign, since expectation is linear and linearity extends to infinite sums.
distractors.misconception: extends linearity from finite to infinite sums without justification

distractors.text: Only for finitely many terms, because infinite sums of random variables have no expectation in general.
distractors.misconception: thinks infinite sums cannot be interchanged even for non-negative terms

distractors.text: Only when the $X_n$ are independent, since dependence would change the value of the expectation.
distractors.misconception: confuses interchange of sum and expectation with independence

distractors.text: Only when $\sum_nX_n$ converges almost surely, which is enough for any sign of the terms.
distractors.misconception: thinks almost sure convergence of the sum guarantees the interchange

distractors.text: Only when every $X_n$ is bounded by one common constant, whatever the sign of the terms.
distractors.misconception: adds a uniform boundedness requirement that is neither necessary nor sufficient

explanation: For $X_n\ge0$ the partial sums increase, so monotone convergence gives the interchange. For signed terms, $\sum E|X_n|<\infty$ lets dominated convergence apply with $Y=\sum|X_n|$.

stem: When are events $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n$ mutually independent?
correct: When $P\big(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\big)=\prod_{i\in I}P(A_i)$ for every subset $I$ of the indices.
When the product rule holds for every finite subfamily, not only for pairs; pairwise independence alone is not enough.

distractors.text: When $P(A_i\cap A_j)=P(A_i)P(A_j)$ for every pair $i\ne j$, since pairs control all the intersections.
distractors.misconception: takes pairwise independence for mutual independence

distractors.text: When the product rule $P(A_1\cap\cdots\cap A_n)=\prod_iP(A_i)$ holds for the full family only.
distractors.misconception: checks only the full intersection and forgets the subfamilies

distractors.text: When the events are pairwise disjoint, since disjoint events share no information with one another.
distractors.misconception: confuses disjointness with independence

distractors.text: When $P(A_i)=P(A_j)$ for all $i,j$, so that no event is more informative than any other.
distractors.misconception: confuses identical probabilities with independence

distractors.text: When $P(A_i\mid A_j)\ge P(A_i)$ for all $i\ne j$, so that no event makes another less likely.
distractors.misconception: replaces independence by non-negative dependence

explanation: Mutual independence needs the product rule for every finite subfamily. Pairwise independence does not imply it, and disjoint events of positive probability are never independent.

stem: Which condition characterises independence of random variables $X$ and $Y$?
correct: $P(X\in A,Y\in B)=P(X\in A)P(Y\in B)$ for all Borel sets $A$ and $B$, i.e. $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ are independent.
The joint law is the product of the marginal laws, which is the same as independence of $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$.

distractors.text: $E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]$, because uncorrelated variables share no information with each other.
distractors.misconception: confuses zero covariance with independence

distractors.text: $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution, so that learning one gives no extra information on the other.
distractors.misconception: confuses identical distribution with independence

distractors.text: $P(X=Y)=0$, since independent variables can almost never take the same value at the same time.
distractors.misconception: invents a condition on coincidence of values

distractors.text: $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)$, which is equivalent to independence.
distractors.misconception: takes additivity of variances, a consequence of zero covariance, for independence

distractors.text: $P(X\le a,Y\le b)=P(X\le a)P(Y\le b)$ for $a=b$ only, since the diagonal determines the rest.
distractors.misconception: checks the product rule on one line instead of all pairs of thresholds

explanation: Independence is the product rule over all Borel sets (equivalently all pairs of thresholds). Zero covariance and additive variances follow from it but do not imply it.

stem: What does the first Borel-Cantelli lemma say?
correct: If $\sum_nP(A_n)<\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$, and no independence of the events is needed.
A summable sequence of probabilities forces almost every outcome to lie in only finitely many of the $A_n$.

distractors.text: If $\sum_nP(A_n)<\infty$ and the events are independent, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$.
distractors.misconception: mixes up the two lemmas and reverses the conclusion

distractors.text: If $\sum_nP(A_n)<\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$ only when the events $A_n$ are independent.
distractors.misconception: adds independence, which this lemma does not need

distractors.text: If $P(A_n)\to0$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$, because the probabilities of single events vanish.
distractors.misconception: replaces summability by $P(A_n)\to0$, which is not enough

distractors.text: If $\sum_nP(A_n)<\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$ only when the events are pairwise disjoint.
distractors.misconception: adds a disjointness requirement

distractors.text: If $\sum_nP(A_n)=\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})>0$, whatever the dependence between the events.
distractors.misconception: states a divergent-sum conclusion that fails without independence

explanation: By countable subadditivity, $P(\limsup A_n)\le\sum_{n\ge N}P(A_n)\to0$. No independence is used; the divergent case is the second lemma and does need it.

stem: What does the second Borel-Cantelli lemma say?
correct: If the events $A_n$ are independent and $\sum_nP(A_n)=\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$.
For independent events with a divergent sum of probabilities, almost every outcome lies in infinitely many $A_n$.

distractors.text: If $\sum_nP(A_n)=\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$, even when the events are strongly dependent.
distractors.misconception: drops independence; e.g. $A_n=A$ with $P(A)=1/2$ gives probability $1/2$

distractors.text: If the events are independent and $\sum_nP(A_n)<\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1$.
distractors.misconception: swaps convergent and divergent sums

distractors.text: If the events are independent and $\sum_nP(A_n)=\infty$, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})>0$ only.
distractors.misconception: underestimates the conclusion; the probability is exactly $1$

distractors.text: If $P(A_n)\to0$ and the events are independent, then $P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0$ in every case.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that $\sum P(A_n)=\infty$ can occur with $P(A_n)\to0$

distractors.text: If the events are independent and $\sum_nP(A_n)=\infty$, then every outcome lies in infinitely many $A_n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses almost sure with sure occurrence

explanation: For independent events, $P(\bigcap_{n\ge N}A_n^c)=\prod_{n\ge N}(1-P(A_n))\le e^{-\sum_{n\ge N}P(A_n)}=0$, so every tail union has probability $1$. Dependence breaks this.

stem: What is the event $\limsup_nA_n=\bigcap_{N\ge1}\bigcup_{n\ge N}A_n$?
correct: The set of outcomes that belong to infinitely many of the events $A_n$.
The event that $A_n$ occurs infinitely often, i.e. for every $N$ some later $A_n$ with $n\ge N$ occurs.

distractors.text: The set of outcomes that belong to all but finitely many of the events $A_n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses limsup with liminf, which is the event of eventually always occurring

distractors.text: The set of outcomes that belong to at least one of the events $A_n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses limsup with the plain union

distractors.text: The set of outcomes that belong to every one of the events $A_n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses limsup with the plain intersection

distractors.text: The set of outcomes that belong to finitely many of the events $A_n$ and then stay out.
distractors.misconception: describes the complement of the limsup event

distractors.text: The set of outcomes that belong to the first event $A_1$ and to infinitely many later events.
distractors.misconception: adds a requirement on the first event

explanation: $\omega\in\bigcap_N\bigcup_{n\ge N}A_n$ means that for each $N$ some $n\ge N$ has $\omega\in A_n$, i.e. infinitely many. The liminf is $\bigcup_N\bigcap_{n\ge N}A_n$: all but finitely many.

stem: Which statement defines $X_n\to X$ almost surely?
correct: $P\big(\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\}\big)=1$: the sequence converges at almost every outcome.
Outside a set of probability zero, the real sequence $X_n(\omega)$ converges to $X(\omega)$.

distractors.text: $P(|X_n-X|>\epsilon)\to0$ for every $\epsilon>0$, so the probability of a large error vanishes.
distractors.misconception: states convergence in probability

distractors.text: $E|X_n-X|\to0$, so the average absolute error vanishes as $n$ grows.
distractors.misconception: states convergence in $L^1$

distractors.text: $P(X_n\le x)\to P(X\le x)$ at every continuity point $x$ of the law of $X$.
distractors.misconception: states convergence in distribution

distractors.text: $X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)$ for every $\omega$ in a set of positive probability, not necessarily $1$.
distractors.misconception: allows the convergence set to have probability below one

distractors.text: $P(|X_n-X|>\epsilon)$ is summable only for some $\epsilon>0$, which already gives convergence.
distractors.misconception: weakens the Borel-Cantelli criterion to a single $\epsilon$

explanation: Almost sure convergence is pointwise convergence on an event of probability one. The other options define convergence in probability, in $L^1$ and in distribution.

stem: Which chain of implications between modes of convergence is correct?
correct: Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution; none of the reverse implications holds in general.
$X_n\to X$ a.s. $\Rightarrow$ in probability $\Rightarrow$ in distribution, and each arrow fails when reversed.

distractors.text: Convergence in distribution implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence almost surely.
distractors.misconception: reverses the whole chain of implications

distractors.text: Convergence in probability implies almost sure convergence, since the probability of an error tends to zero.
distractors.misconception: thinks probability of error vanishing forces pointwise convergence

distractors.text: Convergence almost surely and convergence in $L^1$ are equivalent for every sequence of integrable variables.
distractors.misconception: treats two unrelated modes as equivalent

distractors.text: Convergence in distribution implies convergence in probability whenever the limit is a non-degenerate variable.
distractors.misconception: reverses the true statement that it holds only for constant limits

distractors.text: Convergence almost surely implies convergence in $L^1$ for every sequence, without domination.
distractors.misconception: ignores the counterexample $n1_{(0,1/n)}$

explanation: a.s. implies in probability implies in distribution. Counterexamples: the typewriter sequence converges in probability but not a.s., and $X_n=-X$ with symmetric $X$ converges in distribution but not in probability.

stem: $X_n\to X$ in probability. Which statement about almost sure convergence is correct?
correct: Some subsequence $X_{n_k}$ converges to $X$ almost surely, although the full sequence need not.
One can extract a subsequence that converges almost surely, for instance with $P(|X_{n_k}-X|>2^{-k})$ summable.

distractors.text: The whole sequence $X_n$ converges to $X$ almost surely, since the probability of any error tends to zero.
distractors.misconception: thinks convergence in probability gives a.s. convergence of the full sequence

distractors.text: No subsequence need converge almost surely, since convergence in probability says nothing about outcomes.
distractors.misconception: misses the subsequence result via Borel-Cantelli

distractors.text: Every subsequence of $X_n$ converges to $X$ almost surely, which is why the full sequence does too.
distractors.misconception: overstates the subsequence result to all subsequences

distractors.text: Some subsequence converges to $X$ in $L^1$, because a sequence converging in probability is bounded in $L^1$.
distractors.misconception: claims $L^1$ convergence of a subsequence, which needs integrability assumptions

distractors.text: A subsequence converges almost surely only when the $X_n$ are bounded by a common constant.
distractors.misconception: adds a boundedness requirement

explanation: Choose $n_k$ with $P(|X_{n_k}-X|>2^{-k})<2^{-k}$ and apply the first Borel-Cantelli lemma. The full sequence can fail to converge a.s. (typewriter sequence).

stem: Which statement about convergence in distribution to a constant $c$ is correct?
correct: If $X_n\to c$ in distribution, then $X_n\to c$ in probability; this fails when the limit is not constant.
For a constant limit the two modes coincide, whereas for a random limit only the implication from probability to distribution holds.

distractors.text: If $X_n\to c$ in distribution, then $X_n\to c$ almost surely, because a point mass leaves no room to vary.
distractors.misconception: jumps from distribution to almost sure convergence

distractors.text: Convergence in distribution to $c$ implies convergence in probability only if the $X_n$ are bounded.
distractors.misconception: adds boundedness; none is needed for a constant limit

distractors.text: Convergence in distribution to $c$ implies convergence in $L^1$, so that $E|X_n-c|\to0$.
distractors.misconception: ignores that expectations can fail to converge without uniform integrability

distractors.text: Convergence in distribution to any limit implies convergence in probability, constant or not.
distractors.misconception: overgeneralises from constant to arbitrary limits

distractors.text: Convergence in distribution to $c$ implies nothing about probabilities of large errors $P(|X_n-c|>\epsilon)$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that a point-mass limit pins down tail probabilities

explanation: If the limit is a point mass at $c$, then $P(|X_n-c|>\epsilon)\le 1-F_n(c+\epsilon)+F_n(c-\epsilon)\to0$. For non-constant limits this fails: $X_n=-X$ with symmetric $X$.

stem: How are $L^p$ convergence and convergence in probability related on a probability space?
correct: $L^q$ convergence gives $L^p$ convergence for $p<q$; $L^p$ convergence gives convergence in probability.
Higher moments control lower ones; Markov's inequality turns $L^p$ convergence into convergence in probability.

distractors.text: Convergence in $L^p$ implies convergence in $L^q$ for $q>p$, so lower moments control higher ones.
distractors.misconception: reverses the order of the $L^p$ spaces on a probability space

distractors.text: Convergence in $L^1$ implies almost sure convergence, since small average errors rule out wild paths.
distractors.misconception: confuses $L^1$ with pointwise convergence

distractors.text: Convergence in probability implies convergence in $L^p$ for every $p\ge1$, without further assumptions.
distractors.misconception: reverses the implication; uniform integrability is needed

distractors.text: The inclusion of $L^q$ into $L^p$ for $p<q$ holds on every measure space, finite or infinite.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the inclusion needs a finite measure

distractors.text: Convergence in $L^p$ implies convergence in probability only for $p\ge2$, where Chebyshev applies.
distractors.misconception: thinks Markov's inequality needs $p\ge2$

explanation: On a probability space, $\|Y\|_p\le\|Y\|_q$ for $p<q$ by Jensen/Lyapunov. Markov's inequality then gives convergence in probability from any $L^p$ convergence.

stem: Which statement is the weak law of large numbers for i.i.d. variables $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with partial sums $S_n$?
correct: If $E|X_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=E[X_1]$, then $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability.
The sample mean converges in probability to the common mean $\mu$ when $X_1$ is integrable.

distractors.text: If $E[X_1^2]<\infty$ then $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability, and finite variance is required for it.
distractors.misconception: takes the Chebyshev proof's variance condition for a necessary one

distractors.text: If $E|X_1|<\infty$, then $S_n/n\to\mu$ almost surely, which is the weak form of the law.
distractors.misconception: calls almost sure convergence the weak law

distractors.text: If $E|X_1|<\infty$, then $S_n\to n\mu$ in probability, so that the sums converge themselves.
distractors.misconception: drops the normalisation by $n$; the sums $S_n$ diverge in general

distractors.text: The law holds for every i.i.d. sequence, including standard Cauchy variables, with limit equal to the median.
distractors.misconception: ignores the integrability condition; Cauchy has no mean

distractors.text: If $E|X_1|<\infty$, then $S_n/\sqrt n\to\mu$ in probability, with the usual normalisation.
distractors.misconception: mixes the law of large numbers with the CLT scaling

explanation: WLLN: $S_n/n\to E[X_1]$ in probability when $E|X_1|<\infty$ (finite variance is only a convenient sufficient condition). Cauchy variables have no mean and the law fails.

stem: Which statement is the strong law of large numbers for i.i.d. variables?
correct: If $E|X_1|<\infty$, then $S_n/n\to E[X_1]$ almost surely.
The sample mean converges with probability one to the mean, and integrability of $X_1$ is enough.

distractors.text: If $E[X_1^2]<\infty$ then $S_n/n\to E[X_1]$ almost surely, and finite variance is necessary.
distractors.misconception: adds a variance condition that is not necessary

distractors.text: If $E|X_1|<\infty$ then $S_n/n\to E[X_1]$ in probability only, with no almost sure statement.
distractors.misconception: states the weak law

distractors.text: If $E|X_1|=\infty$ then $S_n/n$ still converges almost surely to some finite limit.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that an infinite mean makes $|S_n|/n\to\infty$ almost surely

distractors.text: If $E|X_1|<\infty$ then $S_n/n\to E[X_1]$ almost surely, but only when the $X_i$ are bounded.
distractors.misconception: adds boundedness

distractors.text: If $E|X_1|<\infty$ then $S_n/n$ converges almost surely, but the limit may be a non-degenerate variable.
distractors.misconception: thinks the limit can be random; by the 0-1 law it is the constant $\mu$

explanation: Kolmogorov's SLLN: for i.i.d. variables, $S_n/n$ converges a.s. iff $E|X_1|<\infty$, and then the limit is $E[X_1]$. Finite variance is not needed.

stem: What happens to the sample mean $\bar X_n$ of $n$ i.i.d. standard Cauchy variables?
correct: $\bar X_n$ is again standard Cauchy for every $n$, so it never settles down: no mean exists.
Averaging does not help: $\bar X_n$ is as spread out as one observation, as $E|X_1|=\infty$.

distractors.text: $\bar X_n\to0$ almost surely, since the Cauchy law is symmetric about $0$ and positive and negative values cancel.
distractors.misconception: uses symmetry to infer a mean; symmetry does not create integrability

distractors.text: $\bar X_n$ converges in probability to the median $0$, with fluctuations of order $1/\sqrt n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sample mean with the sample median

distractors.text: $\bar X_n\to\infty$ almost surely, because the heavy tails push the average upward without bound.
distractors.misconception: thinks heavy tails force divergence to $+\infty$; symmetry rules this out

distractors.text: $\bar X_n$ is asymptotically normal after scaling by $\sqrt n$, because of the central limit theorem.
distractors.misconception: applies the CLT without a finite variance

distractors.text: $\bar X_n$ converges in probability to some constant, but not almost surely.
distractors.misconception: confuses failure of the strong law with failure of the weak law

explanation: The characteristic function of $\bar X_n$ is $(e^{-|t|/n})^n=e^{-|t|}$, so $\bar X_n$ is standard Cauchy for every $n$. No mean exists, so neither law of large numbers applies.

stem: How do the strong and weak laws of large numbers compare?
correct: The strong law gives almost sure convergence of $S_n/n$, which implies the weak law's convergence in probability.
Both concern the sample mean; the strong law holds along almost every path, the weak law only in probability.

distractors.text: The weak law implies the strong law, because convergence in probability is the stronger of the two modes.
distractors.misconception: reverses the implication between the two modes

distractors.text: They are the same statement, since convergence in probability and almost sure convergence coincide for averages.
distractors.misconception: treats the two modes as equivalent

distractors.text: The strong law needs a finite fourth moment, whereas the weak law needs only a finite mean.
distractors.misconception: adds a fourth moment to the strong law; Kolmogorov's version needs only the mean

distractors.text: The weak law concerns the distribution of $S_n$, whereas the strong law concerns its expectation.
distractors.misconception: confuses the two laws with statements about distributions and expectations

distractors.text: The strong law gives a rate of convergence of order $1/\sqrt n$, whereas the weak law gives none.
distractors.misconception: attributes a rate to the strong law; rates come from the CLT or moment bounds

explanation: Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, so the SLLN implies the WLLN under the same moment condition. Neither law gives a rate.

stem: Let $X_i$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2<\infty$. What does Chebyshev's inequality give for $\bar X_n$?
correct: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\epsilon)\le\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}$, which tends to $0$ and proves the weak law.
The variance of $\bar X_n$ is $\sigma^2/n$, so the probability of an $\epsilon$-deviation is at most $\sigma^2/(n\epsilon^2)$.

distractors.text: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\epsilon)\le\dfrac{\sigma^2}{\epsilon^2}$, with no dependence on $n$, so no limit follows.
distractors.misconception: uses the variance of a single observation instead of the mean

distractors.text: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\epsilon)\le\dfrac{n\sigma^2}{\epsilon^2}$, since the variance of a sum grows with $n$.
distractors.misconception: uses the variance of the sum instead of the mean

distractors.text: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\epsilon)\le\dfrac{\sigma}{n\epsilon}$, using the standard deviation in place of the variance.
distractors.misconception: applies Markov's inequality with the wrong power

distractors.text: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\epsilon)\le\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n^2\epsilon^2}$, since the mean divides each term by $n$.
distractors.misconception: divides by $n^2$ and forgets that the variance of the sum is $n\sigma^2$

distractors.text: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\epsilon)\le e^{-n\epsilon^2/(2\sigma^2)}$, which holds for every finite-variance law.
distractors.misconception: states a sub-Gaussian bound that needs exponential moments

explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n$ by independence, and Chebyshev gives $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\epsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)/\epsilon^2=\sigma^2/(n\epsilon^2)$.

stem: Which statement about the characteristic function $\varphi_X(t)=E[e^{itX}]$ is correct?
correct: It exists for every random variable $X$ and every real $t$, satisfies $\varphi_X(0)=1$ and $|\varphi_X(t)|\le1$.
Unlike the moment generating function, it always exists, because $|e^{itX}|=1$.

distractors.text: It exists only for random variables with all moments finite, since it is defined as an expectation.
distractors.misconception: thinks moments are needed; $e^{itX}$ is bounded

distractors.text: It is real-valued for every random variable $X$, which is why it can be compared with the density.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that it is complex-valued unless $X$ is symmetric

distractors.text: It can exceed $1$ in absolute value when $X$ has heavy tails, so the bound $|\varphi_X|\le1$ is not universal.
distractors.misconception: thinks heavy tails break the bound

distractors.text: It is defined as $E[e^{tX}]$ and exists for all real $t$ exactly when $X$ is bounded.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the moment generating function

distractors.text: It is differentiable at $t=0$ for every random variable $X$, with derivative equal to $iE[X]$.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that differentiability at $0$ needs a finite mean (or a symmetric version)

explanation: Because $|e^{itX}|=1$, the expectation always exists and $|\varphi_X|\le1=\varphi_X(0)$. The moment generating function $E[e^{tX}]$ can be infinite.

stem: What does the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions say?
correct: If $\varphi_X=\varphi_Y$ on all of $\mathbb R$, then $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution.
The characteristic function determines the law, so equal characteristic functions mean equal distributions (not equal variables).

distractors.text: If $\varphi_X=\varphi_Y$ on all of $\mathbb R$, then $X=Y$ almost surely, since they carry the same information.
distractors.misconception: confuses equality in law with equality of random variables

distractors.text: The law is determined only when all moments of $X$ exist and the series of moments determines the law.
distractors.misconception: confuses uniqueness of the transform with the moment problem

distractors.text: Two different laws can share a characteristic function if they have the same mean and variance.
distractors.misconception: thinks the first two moments identify the law

distractors.text: The characteristic function determines the law only for laws that have a density with respect to Lebesgue measure.
distractors.misconception: restricts the theorem to absolutely continuous laws

distractors.text: Equal characteristic functions on a small interval around $0$ already give equal laws, for every random variable.
distractors.misconception: thinks local agreement near $0$ is enough in general

explanation: The inversion formula recovers the law from $\varphi$, with no density or moments needed. Equal laws do not make the variables equal.

stem: $X$ and $Y$ are independent. How does the characteristic function of $X+Y$ relate to those of $X$ and $Y$?
correct: $\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)\varphi_Y(t)$ for all real $t$, since the expectation factorises.
The product of the two characteristic functions, so convolution of laws becomes multiplication.

distractors.text: $\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)+\varphi_Y(t)$, since the expectation of a sum is the sum of expectations.
distractors.misconception: applies linearity to the exponential of a sum

distractors.text: $\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)\varphi_Y(t)$ holds for all pairs $X,Y$, independent or not.
distractors.misconception: drops the independence needed for factorisation

distractors.text: $\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)\varphi_Y(t)$ only when $X$ and $Y$ are identically distributed.
distractors.misconception: adds an identical distribution requirement

distractors.text: $\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)\varphi_Y(t)$ only for variables that have finite variance.
distractors.misconception: adds a moment condition that is not needed

distractors.text: $\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)\ast\varphi_Y(t)$, the convolution of the two characteristic functions.
distractors.misconception: mixes up convolution of laws with convolution of transforms

explanation: For independent $X,Y$: $E[e^{itX}e^{itY}]=E[e^{itX}]E[e^{itY}]$. Convolution of laws becomes multiplication of characteristic functions, with no moment conditions.

stem: What does Lévy's continuity theorem say?
correct: $X_n\to X$ in distribution if and only if $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for every real $t$.
Pointwise convergence of the characteristic functions to the characteristic function of $X$ is equivalent to convergence in distribution.

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ almost surely if and only if $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for every real $t$.
distractors.misconception: upgrades convergence in distribution to almost sure convergence

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ in distribution if and only if $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ at $t=0$ only.
distractors.misconception: checks convergence at the single point $t=0$ where all characteristic functions equal $1$

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ in distribution only if $\varphi_{X_n}\to\varphi_X$ uniformly on the whole real line.
distractors.misconception: requires uniform convergence, which is stronger than needed

distractors.text: $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for every $t$ implies $E[X_n]\to E[X]$ for any integrable $X_n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses convergence in distribution with convergence of moments

distractors.text: $X_n\to X$ in probability if and only if $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for every real $t$.
distractors.misconception: confuses convergence in distribution with convergence in probability

explanation: Lévy: convergence in distribution is equivalent to pointwise convergence of characteristic functions (to the characteristic function of a limit). Moments and almost sure behaviour are not controlled.

stem: Which is the characteristic function of $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$?
correct: $\varphi_X(t)=\exp\big(i\mu t-\tfrac12\sigma^2t^2\big)$, a Gaussian in $t$.
$\exp(i\mu t)$ times $\exp(-\sigma^2t^2/2)$: the mean gives the phase, the variance the decay.

distractors.text: $\varphi_X(t)=\exp\big(\mu t+\tfrac12\sigma^2t^2\big)$, the same formula with $i$ removed throughout.
distractors.misconception: gives the moment generating function instead

distractors.text: $\varphi_X(t)=\exp\big(i\mu t+\tfrac12\sigma^2t^2\big)$, which keeps $i$ only on the mean term.
distractors.misconception: gets the sign of the variance term wrong, giving a function unbounded in $t$

distractors.text: $\varphi_X(t)=\exp\big(-\tfrac12\sigma^2t^2\big)$ for every $\mu$, since the mean does not affect the law's shape.
distractors.misconception: drops the phase factor carrying the mean

distractors.text: $\varphi_X(t)=\exp\big(i\mu t-\tfrac12\sigma|t|\big)$, with the standard deviation in place of the variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses the Gaussian with a Cauchy-type exponent linear in $|t|$

distractors.text: $\varphi_X(t)=\dfrac{1}{1+\sigma^2t^2}\,e^{i\mu t}$, a rational function times the phase factor.
distractors.misconception: gives the characteristic function of a Laplace law

explanation: Completing the square gives $E[e^{itX}]=e^{i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2}$. The modulus $e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}$ is at most $1$, in line with $|\varphi|\le1$.

stem: Which statement is the classical central limit theorem for i.i.d. $X_i$ with partial sums $S_n$?
correct: If $E[X_1]=\mu$ and $0<\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)\to N(0,1)$ in distribution.
Finite positive variance suffices: the standardised sum converges in distribution to a standard normal, whatever the law of $X_1$.

distractors.text: If $X_1$ has a finite fourth moment, then $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)\to N(0,1)$, and nothing weaker works.
distractors.misconception: adds a fourth moment condition that is not needed

distractors.text: If $X_1$ is itself normally distributed, then the standardised sum is normal; for other laws it is not.
distractors.misconception: thinks the theorem is only an identity for normal summands

distractors.text: If $E[X_1]=\mu$ is finite, then $(S_n-n\mu)/\sqrt n\to N(0,1)$, with no condition on the variance.
distractors.misconception: drops the variance condition and the standardisation by $\sigma$

distractors.text: If $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)\to N(0,1)$ almost surely.
distractors.misconception: upgrades convergence in distribution to almost sure convergence

distractors.text: If $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma n)\to N(0,1)$ in distribution.
distractors.misconception: uses normalisation by $n$ instead of $\sqrt n$, which gives the law of large numbers

explanation: The classical CLT needs only i.i.d. summands with finite positive variance; the scaling is $\sigma\sqrt n$ and the mode is convergence in distribution.

stem: What does the Lindeberg condition for independent summands $X_{k}$ with total variance $s_n^2$ express?
correct: The share of $s_n^2$ coming from large values $|X_k|>\epsilon s_n$ becomes negligible, so no term dominates.
For every $\epsilon>0$, $s_n^{-2}\sum_kE[X_k^2;\,|X_k|>\epsilon s_n]\to0$: large values carry vanishing variance.

distractors.text: All the summands have the same variance, so that each contributes an equal share of the total variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses the condition with identical variances

distractors.text: All the summands are bounded by one common constant, so that no large value can occur at any stage.
distractors.misconception: takes uniform boundedness, which is sufficient but not the condition

distractors.text: The summands are identically distributed, so that the sum behaves like an i.i.d. sum.
distractors.misconception: confuses the condition with the i.i.d. hypothesis it replaces

distractors.text: The total variance $s_n^2$ converges to a finite limit as $n\to\infty$, so that the sum stays tight.
distractors.misconception: confuses the condition with convergence of the total variance

distractors.text: The summands are independent of the sum $S_n$, so that the sum cannot be affected by a single term.
distractors.misconception: confuses the condition with an independence statement, which is impossible here

explanation: Lindeberg's condition says that, relative to the total variance, large values of individual summands contribute nothing in the limit. It allows different distributions but rules out a dominant term.

stem: Independent, not identically distributed $X_k$ satisfy the Lindeberg condition. What does the Lindeberg-Feller theorem conclude?
correct: $(S_n-E[S_n])/s_n\to N(0,1)$ in distribution, where $s_n^2=\operatorname{Var}(S_n)$.
The standardised sum is asymptotically standard normal, even though the summands have different laws.

distractors.text: $(S_n-E[S_n])/s_n\to N(0,1)$ in distribution, but only if the summands are also identically distributed.
distractors.misconception: insists on identical distributions, which Lindeberg-Feller removes

distractors.text: $(S_n-E[S_n])/s_n\to N(0,1)$ almost surely, since the Lindeberg condition controls the path of the sum.
distractors.misconception: upgrades the mode of convergence to almost sure

distractors.text: $(S_n-E[S_n])/s_n\to N(0,1)$ in distribution, but the result fails for dependent sequences and for independent ones alike.
distractors.misconception: thinks the theorem is never valid

distractors.text: $S_n/n\to E[S_n]/n$ in probability, since the Lindeberg condition gives a law of large numbers.
distractors.misconception: confuses the CLT conclusion with that of a law of large numbers

distractors.text: $(S_n-E[S_n])/s_n$ converges in distribution to a normal law with variance depending on the largest summand.
distractors.misconception: thinks the limit variance depends on a single large summand

explanation: Under Lindeberg's condition the normalised sum is asymptotically $N(0,1)$ for independent, non-identically distributed summands (Feller showed the condition is also necessary when the maximal variance share vanishes).

stem: What does the central limit theorem not tell us about a fixed, finite $n$?
correct: It gives no bound on the error of the normal approximation at fixed $n$; a rate such as Berry-Esseen is a separate result.
It is an asymptotic statement, so accuracy at a particular $n$ depends on the skewness and tails of the summands.

distractors.text: It gives an error of order $1/n$ in the normal approximation for every law with finite variance.
distractors.misconception: states a rate that is wrong; Berry-Esseen gives order $1/\sqrt n$ under a third moment

distractors.text: It guarantees that the normal approximation is exact once $n\ge30$, for any law with a finite mean.
distractors.misconception: turns a rule of thumb into a theorem

distractors.text: It guarantees small relative error in the far tails of $S_n$, because convergence in distribution is uniform in the tails.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that tail probabilities are approximated only with absolute, not relative, accuracy

distractors.text: It says $S_n$ converges to a normal random variable on $\Omega$, so that $S_n$ eventually equals a normal variable.
distractors.misconception: confuses convergence in distribution with convergence of the random variables

distractors.text: It implies that $S_n$ has a density for large $n$ whenever the summands are integer valued.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that sums of integer-valued variables stay discrete

explanation: The CLT is a limit statement. Berry-Esseen gives a uniform error bound of order $1/\sqrt n$ under a finite third moment; accuracy in the tails and for skewed laws can be poor at moderate $n$.

stem: The i.i.d. summands have infinite variance but are symmetric and heavy-tailed. What can be said about the sums $S_n$?
correct: The $\sqrt n$ scaling fails; scaled sums can converge to a non-normal stable law, for example Cauchy.
The classical CLT does not apply, and the scaling and limit depend on the tail index $\alpha$ of the law.

distractors.text: The sums $S_n/\sqrt n$ still converge to a normal law, because symmetry makes the missing variance irrelevant.
distractors.misconception: thinks symmetry can replace a finite variance

distractors.text: The sums $S_n$ must diverge to $+\infty$ almost surely, because heavy tails always push the sum up.
distractors.misconception: ignores symmetry, which prevents divergence to one side

distractors.text: The sums $S_n/n$ converge almost surely to the mean, since the strong law holds for all symmetric laws.
distractors.misconception: applies the strong law to a law with no mean

distractors.text: No scaling of the sums can give a limit in distribution, so no limit theorem exists for such laws.
distractors.misconception: thinks heavy tails rule out all limit theorems

distractors.text: The sums converge in distribution to a normal law, with variance given by the sample variance.
distractors.misconception: replaces the missing population variance by a sample quantity

explanation: With infinite variance, scaled sums can converge to stable laws with scaling $n^{1/\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<2$ (for the Cauchy, $\alpha=1$). The normal limit with $\sqrt n$ is special to finite variance.

stem: What defines the conditional expectation $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ of an integrable $X$ given a sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal G$?
correct: The $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ with $E[Z1_G]=E[X1_G]$ for all $G\in\mathcal G$; it exists by Radon-Nikodym.
A $\mathcal G$-measurable variable with the same integrals as $X$ over every event of $\mathcal G$, unique up to null sets.

distractors.text: The constant $E[X]$, since averaging over $\mathcal G$ removes all the randomness that $\mathcal G$ can see.
distractors.misconception: confuses a conditional expectation with the unconditional one

distractors.text: The value $E[X\mid G]$ computed pointwise for each outcome $\omega$, as $E[X\mid\{\omega\}]$, which is always defined.
distractors.misconception: conditions on null events; $P(\{\omega\})$ may be zero

distractors.text: The variable $X$ itself whenever $X$ is integrable, since $X$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal F\supseteq\mathcal G$.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that $X$ need not be $\mathcal G$-measurable

distractors.text: A $\mathcal G$-measurable variable $Z$ that is unique everywhere on $\Omega$, not only up to null sets.
distractors.misconception: claims uniqueness everywhere rather than almost surely

distractors.text: Any $\mathcal G$-measurable variable with $E[Z]=E[X]$; matching the overall mean is the whole requirement.
distractors.misconception: checks only the total mean, not the integrals over every event of $\mathcal G$

explanation: $Z=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable with $E[Z1_G]=E[X1_G]$ for all $G\in\mathcal G$. Existence comes from Radon-Nikodym, uniqueness only up to null sets.

stem: For $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$, what does the tower property say?
correct: $E\big[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H\big]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$: the coarser $\sigma$-algebra wins.
The coarser conditioning absorbs the finer one, so the tower collapses to $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

distractors.text: $E\big[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H\big]=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$, so the finer conditioning is the one that survives.
distractors.misconception: keeps the finer $\sigma$-algebra instead of the coarser one

distractors.text: $E\big[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\big]=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$, so a second expectation changes nothing.
distractors.misconception: confuses the unconditional expectation with a conditional one

distractors.text: $E\big[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H\big]=E[X\mid\mathcal G]\,E[X\mid\mathcal H]$, the product of the two.
distractors.misconception: replaces iteration by a product

distractors.text: $E\big[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H\big]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ only when $\mathcal G$ and $\mathcal H$ are independent.
distractors.misconception: adds independence, when nesting is what is needed

distractors.text: $E\big[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H\big]=E[X\mid\mathcal G\cup\mathcal H]$, which combines both pieces of information.
distractors.misconception: thinks iterated conditioning merges the two $\sigma$-algebras

explanation: Because $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$, the coarser information wins. With $\mathcal H=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$ this is the law of total expectation.

stem: $Y$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $X$, $XY$ are integrable. What is $E[XY\mid\mathcal G]$?
correct: $Y\,E[X\mid\mathcal G]$: a $\mathcal G$-measurable factor can be taken out of the conditional expectation.
The known factor $Y$ comes out, leaving the conditional expectation of the other factor $X$ given $\mathcal G$.

distractors.text: $E[Y]\,E[X\mid\mathcal G]$, since $Y$ must be replaced by its mean before it comes out.
distractors.misconception: replaces the known variable by a constant

distractors.text: $E[Y\mid\mathcal G]\,E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for all integrable pairs $X$ and $Y$, whether $Y$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable or not.
distractors.misconception: factorises for arbitrary pairs; this holds only when one factor is measurable or conditionally independent

distractors.text: $Y\,E[X]$, because conditioning removes all the dependence on $X$ that $\mathcal G$ could have seen.
distractors.misconception: drops the conditioning on one factor

distractors.text: $E[XY]$, a constant, since conditional expectations of products are unconditional expectations.
distractors.misconception: replaces the conditional expectation by the unconditional expectation

distractors.text: $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ only, because the factor $Y$ affects the answer only through $\mathcal G$.
distractors.misconception: drops the known factor altogether

explanation: Taking out what is known: if $Y$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable (and the products are integrable) then $E[XY\mid\mathcal G]=Y\,E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

stem: $X$ is integrable and independent of $\mathcal G$. What is $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$?
correct: The constant $E[X]$, since $\mathcal G$ carries no information about $X$.
$E[X\mid\mathcal G]=E[X]$ almost surely, as $E[X1_G]=E[X]P(G)=E[E[X]1_G]$ for $G\in\mathcal G$.

distractors.text: The variable $X$ itself, because $X$ is integrable and conditioning on $\mathcal G$ leaves it unchanged.
distractors.misconception: keeps $X$; this requires $X$ to be $\mathcal G$-measurable

distractors.text: The constant $0$, because independent variables have no conditional mean to speak of.
distractors.misconception: confuses independence with a zero conditional mean

distractors.text: It is not defined, because conditioning on a $\sigma$-algebra independent of $X$ gives no valid candidate.
distractors.misconception: thinks independence makes the conditional expectation undefined

distractors.text: A non-constant $\mathcal G$-measurable variable with the same mean as $X$, but nothing more.
distractors.misconception: denies that the answer is constant

distractors.text: The constant $E[X]$ only when $\mathcal G$ is the trivial $\sigma$-algebra $\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$.
distractors.misconception: restricts the result to the trivial $\sigma$-algebra

explanation: The constant $E[X]$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and satisfies $E[E[X]1_G]=E[X]P(G)=E[X1_G]$ by independence, so it is the conditional expectation.

stem: For $X\in L^2$, what is the optimality property of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$?
correct: Among all $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z\in L^2$, it minimises $E[(X-Z)^2]$: it is the orthogonal projection of $X$ onto $L^2(\mathcal G)$.
It is the best mean-square predictor of $X$ that uses only the information in $\mathcal G$.

distractors.text: Among all $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$, it minimises $E|X-Z|$, the mean absolute error.
distractors.misconception: confuses the conditional mean with the conditional median

distractors.text: Among all linear functions of the generators of $\mathcal G$, it is the best predictor, and no non-linear one does better.
distractors.misconception: thinks the best predictor is linear; the projection is over all measurable functions

distractors.text: Among all $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$, it minimises $\operatorname{Var}(Z)$, giving the least spread among predictors.
distractors.misconception: confuses minimal prediction error with minimal variance of the predictor

distractors.text: Among all $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$, it minimises $\operatorname{ess\,sup}|X-Z|$, the worst-case error.
distractors.misconception: confuses the $L^2$ projection with a sup-norm approximation

distractors.text: Among all $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$, it maximises the correlation of $Z$ with the original $X$ at fixed mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses projection with a correlation criterion that does not fix the scale

explanation: In $L^2$, $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is the orthogonal projection onto the closed subspace $L^2(\mathcal G)$, hence the unique minimiser of the mean-square error among $\mathcal G$-measurable predictors.

stem: What defines a martingale $(M_n)$ with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)$?
correct: $M_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and integrable, and $E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=M_n$ almost surely for every $n$.
The process is adapted, integrable, and its conditional expected next value, given the past, equals its present value.

distractors.text: $M_n$ is adapted and integrable, and $E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge M_n$ almost surely for every $n$.
distractors.misconception: describes a submartingale rather than a martingale

distractors.text: $M_n$ is adapted and integrable, and only the unconditional means are constant: $E[M_n]=E[M_0]$ for all $n$.
distractors.misconception: replaces the conditional condition by constant means, which is much weaker

distractors.text: $M_n$ has independent increments with mean zero, and every martingale must have this structure.
distractors.misconception: thinks a martingale must have independent increments

distractors.text: $M_n$ is bounded and $E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=M_n$ almost surely, so that boundedness is part of the definition.
distractors.misconception: adds boundedness to the definition

distractors.text: $M_n$ is adapted and $E[M_{n+1}-M_n\mid\mathcal F_n]=0$ only on the event $\{M_n\ge0\}$.
distractors.misconception: restricts the martingale property to a part of the sample space

explanation: A martingale is adapted, integrable and satisfies $E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=M_n$. Independent increments give martingales (with mean zero) but are not required.

stem: What makes a random time $T$ with values in $\{0,1,2,\dots,\infty\}$ a stopping time for $(\mathcal F_n)$?
correct: $\{T\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$: whether we have stopped by time $n$ is decided by information up to time $n$.
The decision to stop at time $n$ uses only the past and present, never the future of the process.

distractors.text: $\{T\le n\}\in\mathcal F_\infty$ for every $n$, so that the decision may use the whole path of the process.
distractors.misconception: allows the decision to use future information

distractors.text: $T$ is a deterministic constant, since only a constant time can be known at each stage.
distractors.misconception: restricts stopping times to constants

distractors.text: $T$ is finite almost surely, so that the process is stopped at some random but finite time.
distractors.misconception: confuses being a stopping time with being finite

distractors.text: $T$ is independent of the process $(M_n)$, so that the stopping rule does not use the process at all.
distractors.misconception: confuses stopping times with times independent of the process

distractors.text: $T$ is the time at which the whole path attains its maximum, since that is a well-defined random time.
distractors.misconception: gives a time that requires knowing the future of the path

explanation: A stopping time is adapted: $\{T\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$. The first hitting time of a set is one; the time of the overall maximum is not, since it needs the future.

stem: Which condition guarantees the optional stopping identity $E[M_T]=E[M_0]$ for a martingale $(M_n)$ and a stopping time $T$?
correct: $T$ is bounded, or $T<\infty$ a.s. with the stopped process dominated by an integrable variable.
Bounded $T$ suffices; otherwise domination or uniform integrability of the stopped process is needed.

distractors.text: $T<\infty$ almost surely, and nothing more is required since the stopped value $M_T$ is then well defined.
distractors.misconception: takes almost sure finiteness for a sufficient condition

distractors.text: $E[T]<\infty$ alone, with no condition on the increments of the martingale.
distractors.misconception: drops the increment condition; $E[T]<\infty$ needs bounded increments

distractors.text: $M_n\ge0$ for every $n$, which turns the identity into an equality instead of an inequality.
distractors.misconception: thinks non-negativity gives equality; Fatou gives only $E[M_T]\le E[M_0]$

distractors.text: $T$ is independent of $(M_n)$, which is the only case in which the identity can hold.
distractors.misconception: confuses the condition with independence of the stopping time

distractors.text: No condition at all: $E[M_T]=E[M_0]$ for every stopping time of every martingale.
distractors.misconception: believes optional stopping is unconditional

explanation: For bounded $T$ the identity always holds. For unbounded $T$ it needs extra control, for instance a dominated or uniformly integrable stopped process; $T<\infty$ a.s. alone is not enough.

stem: A simple symmetric random walk $S_n$ starts at $0$ and $T=\inf\{n:S_n=1\}$. What does this example show?
correct: $T<\infty$ a.s. yet $E[S_T]=1\ne0=E[S_0]$: the stopped walk is not uniformly integrable.
An a.s. finite stopping time can break the identity when uniform integrability fails.

distractors.text: The walk is not a martingale, since its expected value changes at the stopping time $T$.
distractors.misconception: concludes the walk is not a martingale, though $S_n$ is one

distractors.text: $T$ is not a stopping time, because it depends on the whole path of the walk.
distractors.misconception: thinks a hitting time depends on the future; it is adapted

distractors.text: $T=\infty$ with positive probability, so that $S_T$ is undefined on a set of positive probability.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that the symmetric walk hits $1$ almost surely

distractors.text: Optional stopping holds here with $E[S_T]=0$, because $T$ is almost surely finite.
distractors.misconception: takes almost sure finiteness for sufficient; here $S_T=1$ exactly

distractors.text: $E[T]<\infty$ here, which is why the stopped walk keeps its mean at the value $1$.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that $E[T]=\infty$ for this hitting time

explanation: $S_T=1$ almost surely, so $E[S_T]=1$, while $E[S_0]=0$. The stopped walk $S_{n\wedge T}$ is a martingale with mean $0$ but is not uniformly integrable, and $E[T]=\infty$.

stem: A fair $\pm1$ random walk $S_n$ starts at $i$, with $0<i<N$, and $T$ is the first time it hits $0$ or $N$. How does optional stopping give the probability of reaching $N$?
correct: $S_{n\wedge T}$ is a bounded martingale, so $E[S_T]=i$, and with $p=P(S_T=N)$ we get $pN=i$ and $p=i/N$.
Because the stopped walk stays within $[0,N]$, optional stopping applies and $E[S_T]=i$ yields the ruin probabilities.

distractors.text: Optional stopping cannot be used, because $T$ is unbounded and so the identity $E[S_T]=i$ must fail.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that boundedness of the stopped process, not of $T$, is what is used

distractors.text: Optional stopping gives $E[S_T]=0$ for every starting point $i$, so that $p=0$.
distractors.misconception: applies the identity with the wrong starting value

distractors.text: Optional stopping gives $E[S_T]=i$, and since $S_T$ takes only two values, $p=1/2$ for every $i$.
distractors.misconception: concludes by symmetry that the two exits are equally likely, ignoring the start

distractors.text: Optional stopping gives $p=i/(N-i)$, the ratio of the distance to $0$ to the distance to $N$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the probability with an odds ratio

distractors.text: Optional stopping gives $E[S_T]=i$ only if $E[T]<\infty$ is known first, which must be proved separately.
distractors.misconception: thinks finiteness of $E[T]$ is needed when the stopped walk is bounded

explanation: The stopped walk is a bounded martingale, so dominated convergence gives $E[S_T]=\lim E[S_{n\wedge T}]=i$. Then $NP(S_T=N)=i$, hence $P(S_T=N)=i/N$.
